newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bangkok looks to Hong Kong's Wu to ease traffic.
newsitem.headline: Bangkok looks to Hong Kong's Wu to ease traffic.

text.p: Legend has it that 10 years ago Hong Kong magnate Gordon Wu was so frustrated by a drive through traffic from Bangkok's Don Muang airport to the city center that he resolved to build the city a mass transit system.

Wu, chairman of Hopewell Holdings Ltd, drove that route into town once again last week to explain to newly-appointed Transport Minister Suwat Liptapallop just when his long-delayed $3.2 billion mass transit system would be ready.

After a contract signing between Wu and Thailand in 1991, the project has been hit by serious delays that Wu blames on government bungling and red tape, and the Thai government blames on Wu's failure to provide project financing.

But Hopewell executives told Reuters the financing now seems to be in place and the prospect of not just Hopewell's scheme but two other mass transit projects being in place by 2002 appears more real than ever.
Despite government threats to scrap the project should Hopewell fail to elevate much of Bangkok's existing rail network over the next two years, Wu was upbeat following his meeting.
"What delay? The project will be finished before the (1998) Asian Games. Don't listen to other people," Wu told Reuters on Friday after briefing Suwat on plans to speed up construction.
Bob Kevorkian, managing director of Philipp Holzmann (Thai), Hopewell's major project contractor, described Friday's meeting as "very positive".
He said Wu told the minister that 18 billion baht ($750 million) of money raised by sale of shares in Hopewell's Hong Kong subsidiary Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd would go to the project.
That would take registered capital in Hopewell (Thailand) Ltd, the firm responsible for the project, from 12 billion baht to 30 billion baht over the next nine months, he said.
Combined with money pledged by German bank KFW and Siemens AG, which is helping provide the train system, Wu now appears to have enough in hand to fund the delayed project.

With completion of an overhead rail system three years away, and construction on the city's first subway also under way, transit executives believe the completion of Hopewell's elevated rail and road system could at last offer Bangkok residents some respite from the city's congestion.

"It's going to make a huge difference. In the space of the last 12 months we have moved to a situation where we could see three complementary systems in Bangkok operational within the space of three years," said Howard Brooke, senior vice-president at Bangkok Mass Transit System, which is building the overhead rail system.

Over those 12 months a contract was awarded and work begun on the city's first subway line. Continuing construction and the final financing tranche for the overhead rail system should see that the first project is finished by January 2000.
If Wu's reaffirmed commitment to finish the Hopewell project can now be translated into steel and concrete, the question is less if, but when the other projects will be operational.
Passenger projections for the overhead rail system are based on Hopewell's system, and the subway, being operational in January 2002, Brooke said.
That is forecast to take between 10 percent and 20 percent of all journeys off the roads and onto mass transit systems.
Even so it seems there is no guarantee that Bangkok's formidable traffic will see a solution anytime soon.

"I don't want to be overly pessimistic but our international experience shows it (mass transit) has little effect. If it leaves a vacuum on the road, then someone jumps in a car and fills it," Brooke said.
